newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee up sharply, July/Sept switch balloons.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee up sharply, July/Sept switch balloons.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures remained sharply higher at midday, with the nearby July/September switch bulging amid continuing supply concerns, traders said.

Traders said keen commission house buying of the July/September switch, a barometer of nearby supplies, pushed it out to a hefty 35.00 cents per lb as of 1224 EDT from 30.80 cents at the close on Friday.
"The story remains the same: inadequate supply," said one trader. "And as long as it remains, we will continue to see a squeeze on the front month."

The benchmark July contract surged to a new life-of-contract high of 269.50 cents before light profit-taking trimmed gains. At 1224, July stood at 267.00 cents, up 10.15 cents. Second-month September was 5.70 higher, at 231.75, while the back months were up 1.00 to 5.00.

Coffee prices slumped at the opening after some speculative longs liquidated their positions on reports top-grower Brazil had made it through the weekend without any crop-damaging cold weather, traders said.

But good interest at the dips limited losses and disappointed locals were forced to cover short positions, they said. Upward momentum accelerated after the July contract blew through resistance at 262.00, the 265.00, activating buy-stops and encountering little in the way of any selling, they said.
"There are a lack of sellers in this market," a trader said. "Nothing is stopping it right now."

New York coffee futures have been on a tear since the end of last year -- more than doubling in price -- as worries about low inventory levels were exacerbated by forecasts for smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries.
Other concerns leading to price pressure are labor unrest in Colombia and Brazil and projections for a smaller crop in top-grower Brazil in the coming 1997/98 season.

The market continues to recieve underlying support from the supply woes as well as the approach of the Brazilian winter, with any signs of cool weather likely to spark nervous buying. Two severe frosts in 1994, one in June and another in July, damaged some Brazil's coffee trees and sent world prices spinning higher.
